title: LawNext on Location: The View from Tiburon – A Conversation with Pablo Arredondo, Casetext Cofounder
author: Pablo Arredondo

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: Arredondo endorses continued agentic development but reframes the central advance as reasoning models and the transfer of verifiable-reward capabilities from coding into knowledge work. He does not substantively address the cluster’s core concerns about autonomy levels, error propagation, human intervention or verification bottlenecks, and offers no measured legal-work evidence.
qs: Agentic is a word that you've learned around, okay fine, but really this was that next thing.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: Arredondo expects reasoning and coding-agent capabilities to transfer into knowledge work, but the excerpt does not address whether legal value depends on expert-designed workflows, client context, tacit-knowledge transfer or retained human checkpoints. It therefore neither clearly accepts nor rejects the cluster’s principal proposition.
qs: And now what's happening is the coding agents, the fact that even though you can only, so reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards, right?

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Arredondo discusses legal AI’s adoption lag, future capability gains, reasoning models and agentic techniques, but does not address associate apprenticeship, the verification-experience paradox, or measures to preserve expertise reproduction. His expectation of broader economic change is only tangential to the cluster proposition.

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: Arredondo supports the adjacent distinction between rapid adoption and realised transformation, noting that expected economic change has not yet occurred and suggesting implementation may delay gains. However, he does not address access to justice, legal-aid capacity or whether AI can close justice gaps, so his position on the cluster’s principal proposition cannot be determined.
qs: First, you actually have this dip because people are trying to apply it clumsily and they don't know how to do it and it's rolling out and then you start to see the gains.

st.t: Vertical AI: Commercial traction cannot prove defensibility
st.an: Arredondo accepts that a specialist legal-AI company can create acquisition value through a head start and brand, while adding concrete evidence that a content-rich incumbent could also develop strong legal AI internally and hedge through simultaneous building and buying. This strengthens the cluster’s conclusion that commercial value and early advantage do not by themselves establish durable defensibility.
qs: They were going to be releasing fantastic LLM-based legal research, whether they bought us or not.
But I think we did have a big head start with it.

st.t: Adoption leadership: Trust must follow customer outcomes
st.an: Arredondo supports the cluster’s cautious, iterative approach to adoption by stressing that product experiments can fail and startups must remain able to adapt. His contribution is experience-based advice rather than demonstrated transformation or systematic evidence, and it does not directly address customer outcomes or distributed leadership.
qs: But yes, you do need to be able to to pivot and adjust and that's one of the great things about startups.

st.t: Harvey strategy: Prestige supports infrastructure ambitions
st.an: Arredondo supports the cluster’s market-traction proposition by treating Harvey’s fundraising and valuation as credible and praising its work and talent. His comments offer informed industry validation, but no comparative evidence on accuracy, productivity, workflow infrastructure, governance or durable defensibility.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s account that GPT-4 marked a capability threshold for specialist legal AI and that useful legal products emerged through sustained iteration rather than foundation-model access alone. However, it offers development anecdotes, not evidence about human verification, comparative performance or the durability of specialist workflow layers.
qs: And I just say that because I love talking about just watching this technology grow from those sort of early precursors to then GPT-4, which is what Co-Council was anchored in.
So if you add it all together, it's basically been 16 years of pretty nonstop pursuit of it, which So makes it all the more sweeter.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s cautious account of an immature transition: legal AI adoption is unusually rapid, but tools remain underdeveloped, reliable usage evidence is lacking, and anticipated changes to billing and legal-service economics have not yet materialised. It does not directly address the cluster’s fuller claims about hybrid pricing, buyer-side reallocation or provider restructuring.
qs: I all of these tools, we're so far from where I think we're going to be.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Arredondo aligns with the cluster’s core proposition: legal AI has broad and consequential capabilities, but current limitations, slow institutional adoption, incomplete workflow integration, trustworthy content infrastructure and human verification constrain realised value. His call to monitor systemic side effects also fits the cluster’s continuous, use-context-specific governance approach.
qs: They're using the right models and they're checking their work.
Doing all this stuff, it's critical and it's a lot harder.

kp.k: General-purpose models consolidated previously separate legal product opportunities
kp.d: Arredondo recalls that Casetext obtained early GPT-4 access on September 16th, 2022, before ChatGPT's release, and built the skills that became Co-Counsel. He describes identifying approximately 74 use cases, including deposition summarisation and transcript outlines, each of which could previously have supported a separate company. This is a founder's retrospective account of expanding technical capabilities and blurred product boundaries, not a measured market study.
qs: Can you summarize a depot? Can you make a transcript outline? Can you? And each of those would be a company in the old world.

We got to see, and I think I counted at the end, we had 74. something like that where I was like, these are individual use cases, any one of which I would run excitedly to tell somebody that we built.

kp.k: Adoption and economic change lagged founders' expectations
kp.d: Looking back roughly three years after Co-Counsel's launch, Arredondo says he and Jake expected AI use to have become effectively universal among attorneys. He nevertheless describes adoption as exceptionally fast for legal technology, acknowledges continuing profound model limitations, and notes that billing rates are still rising. He invokes economists' innovation J-curve as a possible explanation for delayed gains, without supplying adoption percentages or productivity measurements.
qs: I think we would have thought it would just be unheard of for attorneys to not be using this.
They still have some profound ones, but even more so then.
First, you actually have this dip because people are trying to apply it clumsily and they don't know how to do it and it's rolling out and then you start to see the gains.

kp.k: Reported judicial test results require substantial attribution caution
kp.d: Arredondo reports a recent University of Chicago study associated with Eric Posner that revived a 1960s judicial-competence study. He describes testing whether pro-plaintiff or pro-defendant wording changes answers to otherwise identical facts, and recalls judges answering correctly 62% of the time versus AI scoring 100%. He explicitly qualifies his recollection and urges reading the study; the transcript provides no sample size, model identity or methodological detail sufficient to generalise to judicial work.
qs: So they revived an earlier study from the 60s that was testing judicial competence, giving them questions.
you know, always with all of these grain of salt, any study, go read the study itself.
But I believe the headline was the judges were correct 62 % of the time and the AI actually scored 100%.

kp.k: Verification does not exhaust legal AI's systemic risks
kp.d: Arredondo distinguishes fabricated-output incidents and failures to read briefs from subtler consequences of successful AI use. He says good attorneys use appropriate models and check their work, but argues that researchers must also examine aggregate, unintended effects on legal language. He reports discussions with BYU's Center for Computational Linguistics about establishing a project to monitor statistical changes in the common law, including word length, variation and dashes; no results are presented.
qs: They're using the right models and they're checking their work.
But what about when it's working? and it's going well, what are the other things that are happening?

So I've been talking with folks at BYU's Center for Computational Linguistics to set up a project where all we're going to do is just monitor the common law to look, are there statistical differences? Is the word length changing? Is the variation changing? Are there more dashes?

kp.k: Acquisition combined AI capabilities with incumbent content and scale
kp.d: The host dates Co-Counsel's debut to March 1st, 2023 and describes Thomson Reuters acquiring Casetext about four months later for $650 million. Arredondo says Casetext had not solved its content needs, regards reliable legal content as difficult and essential, and describes the acquisition as a difficult but unregretted choice. His explanation of Thomson Reuters' motives is expressly interpretive: GPT-4 represented a major change worth securing options around. Separately, the host reports executives describing simultaneous building and buying as hedging their bets.
qs: the content, the truth is we didn't solve content in any real way.
I think that the truth is the less glamorous stuff of actually making the content really reliable and trustworthy. Doing all this stuff, it's critical and it's a lot harder. than it seems.
And their answer was we were kind of hedging our bets. We were both building and buying at the same time.

kp.k: Foundation-model providers threaten legal vendors' feature differentiation
kp.d: Arredondo argues that Anthropic, DeepMind and OpenAI have become materially relevant competitors to legal technology providers. Using a reported Claude Cowork review mentioning Bates stamping, he explains that general systems can supply formerly specialised features without deliberately targeting legal markets. He calls this a fundamental competitive threat, while predicting benefits for lawyers and justice from increased competition; these benefits are expectations, not demonstrated outcomes.
qs: when you look at it coming like Anthropic and DeepMind and OpenAI, they're now relevant to legal tech in a way that we're not, the field wasn't used to, or the industry really wasn't used to in the past.
It's because somebody asked it to, so it does.
It's a fundamental shift, right? So absolutely it's a threat. For lawyers, it's great. For justice, it's great. It means that there's going to be a lot more competition.

kp.k: Specialisation must demonstrate value beyond foundation-model capabilities
kp.d: Arredondo recommends that legal vendors attempt their own workflows using general-purpose systems and ask what their products add. He predicts continued opportunities for tailored legal systems, particularly through reinforcement-learning approaches, but doubts that the initial wave of fine-tuned models necessarily established that advantage. He rejects the host's framing of Harvey's fundraising and valuation as necessarily crazy and praises its work without treating it as the sole solution.
qs: Even more amazing and finding tailored systems. I don't think the first wave of fine-tune models necessarily did that
And if it's nothing, then you have to ask yourself some hard questions about what you can do.
are they the only solution? No, of course not.

kp.k: Reliable, complete legal content remains a competitive advantage
kp.d: Arredondo argues that content cannot always be obtained simply by sending an agent to collect it: achieving completeness may require courthouse access. He praises aggregation efforts while recognising that barriers should be reduced. He also suggests that models do not yet reproduce the quality of specialised treatises and that the importance of such material depends on the matter. He allows that some incumbent content advantages may erode rather than claiming permanent protection.
qs: think some of that content isn't as easy as go send an agent to get it.
But the difference between 90 percent and sort of 100 percent, some of the stuff I think people have to go to the courthouse to get.
So it depends on your matter maybe what you're working on but I think content is still king and maybe context is now queen.

kp.k: Global deployment adds constraints absent from startup prototyping
kp.d: Reflecting on Thomson Reuters, Arredondo distinguishes small-team experimentation from deploying products internationally across different rules, regulations and server requirements. He says global-scale innovation is harder and that rapid decisions changing an entire product line are less available than in a startup. Nonetheless, he reports being given space for a small prototyping team and praises the organisation's expertise and response to language models.
qs: what it really means to be a global company with each different country's rules and regulations and servers and things like that.
it's very different to do it for real for the whole world
you're saying you're going to put it out at scale again around the entire world. Yes, that's harder.

kp.k: Workflow integration should remove manual document transfers
kp.d: Arredondo supports Co-Counsel's direction and praises deep-research-based legal research, but wants a more unified environment connecting research materials and working files. He identifies downloading documents from a docket and dragging them into another system as unnecessary human work that integrated tools should eliminate. This is a product-development recommendation rather than evidence of measured labour savings.
qs: All of it I want to be much more unified.
seeing the gold standard for research now become a research, a deep research based system. That's been incredible to see.
you have to download documents from a docket and then go take it and drag it over there. Well, come on now, just take it right from the docket, right?

kp.k: Reasoning and coding agents enable broader knowledge-work automation
kp.d: Arredondo identifies reasoning models as the major advance after GPT-4 and describes coding-agent capabilities transferring into legal tasks. He attributes improved tool use and spontaneous system self-checking to reinforcement learning, particularly learning from verifiable rewards in mathematics and coding. He anticipates further legal products from this approach but gives no performance measurements; the systems' self-checking is distinct from human verification of legal output.
qs: the next big jump was really the reasoning models
So reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards, right? So like math and coding.
you can give it legal tasks and it basically says, right, let me show you how I would code, quote unquote, code this.
the ability of these systems to, through reinforcement learning, become so good at tool calling and spontaneously checking their work

kp.k: Eviction-appeal pilot supported time-sensitive judicial processing
kp.d: Arredondo describes working with Justice Green and staff at the Massachusetts Court of Appeals during the GPT-4 period on emergency eviction appeals. The system organised internal filings into summaries and checked another database. He reports that Green authorised him to call the project a success, but supplies no case count, time savings, accuracy results or evidence of improved litigant outcomes.
qs: We worked with the Massachusetts Court of Appeals, Justice Green.
We took emergency eviction appeals.
Like just created a kind of organized summary, went to another database to check things.
He told me, like, you're allowed to say that that is a success.

kp.k: Opinion drafting raises concerns beyond efficiency and accuracy
kp.d: Arredondo says work with other judges expanded over the preceding year and a half into bench memoranda and opinion drafting. He describes initial reluctance to go beyond bench memos, then reconsideration in response to trial judges reporting overwhelming workloads. He distinguishes those pressures from appellate judges' concerns and expresses no settled answer about appropriate use. Judicial attitudes range from active experimentation to rejection, with clerks adding another layer of adoption.
qs: over the last year and a half, and this is with other judges, we've gone further into like bench memos, and then even into drafting of opinions.
my thinking evolved on it from kind of saying no we're not we'll do bench memos but that's as far as i want to go
No, we are so swamped. We're so overburdened.
not just look at, you know, is it getting the thing wrong or does it save 10 minutes or not, but like, what is the aggregate effect of having it?

kp.k: Legal product development required adaptation rather than straightforward scaling
kp.d: Arredondo describes Casetext's initial crowdsourced legal annotations as unsuccessful despite the apparent analogy to engineers' Stack Overflow participation. The company instead imported lawyers' client alerts and attached them to cases. His broader advice is to combine resilience, genuine subject-matter commitment, complementary co-founders and willingness to pivot. He notes that earlier investments in a case-law database supported later brief analysis, illustrating continuity across some product changes rather than wholesale reinvention.
qs: The idea was always sound and it worked so well for engineers with like stack overflow. It just wasn't the right thing for law for lawyers.
So we still got to that idea of having an annotated case law, but just not in the sort of community based system that we originally had hoped.
It was still because we had built a case law database that we could then go and do this.
you do need to be able to to pivot and adjust and that's one of the great things about startups.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Pablo Arredondo describes broadly capable AI that consolidates legal-software functions, intensifies competition, improves research and judicial workflows, and introduces unresolved systemic risks.
pts.d:
1. Arredondo says GPT-4's general capabilities enabled dozens of legal use cases, including deposition summaries and transcript outlines, that previously could each have supported a separate company. AI consequently blurs traditional product boundaries.
2. He says adoption and profession-wide change have fallen short of his and his cofounder's early expectations, despite adoption being faster than previous legal technologies. They had expected non-use by attorneys to become exceptional; he observes that billing rates are still increasing rather than exhibiting the change they anticipated. He suggests, rather than establishes, that an innovation J-curve may explain delayed gains.
3. He argues that foundation-model companies and general-purpose agents now pose a fundamental competitive threat to specialist legal-tech vendors. Features formerly requiring dedicated product development can become available simply because users request them. He expects greater competition to benefit lawyers and justice, without specifying or measuring an access-to-justice outcome.
4. He does not regard this threat as necessarily fatal to specialist providers. Tailored legal systems, potentially strengthened by reinforcement learning, and reliable legal content can still differentiate them. He says early fine-tuning efforts did not necessarily supply that differentiation. Comprehensive case-law collections and authoritative treatises remain difficult to reproduce, although some content advantages may erode.
5. He characterizes deep-research systems as a major advance in legal research and argues that legal workflows remain insufficiently integrated. Routine manual transfers, such as downloading docket documents and uploading them elsewhere, should give way to direct retrieval within the workflow.
6. He identifies reasoning models and the transfer of coding-agent capabilities into knowledge work as successive advances. He says reinforcement learning supports better tool use and spontaneous checking by systems, and anticipates further legal applications, including from Thomson Reuters. This is a claim about system capabilities, not a claim that human verification is unnecessary.
7. He reports that a Massachusetts emergency-eviction-appeals workflow, which organized filings into summaries and checked another database, was successful. He describes subsequent work with other judges on bench memoranda and opinion drafting. He regards judicial drafting as especially consequential and says overloaded trial courts may face a different benefit-risk calculation from appellate courts.
8. He argues that checking for fabricated material or counting minutes saved is insufficient to assess AI's effects on the judiciary. Even functioning systems may alter the common law's language or other aggregate characteristics. He describes a proposed monitoring project, not demonstrated changes. He also observes a wide range of judicial attitudes, from sophisticated adoption to complete rejection.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims primarily rest on Arredondo's product-development and judicial-collaboration experience, supplemented by a product review, a cautiously recalled study, and expectations rather than measured market outcomes.
pts.d:
For the breadth and consolidation of legal functions, Arredondo offers firsthand experience testing early GPT-4 and developing CoCounsel, including an approximate count of 74 use cases; he supplies no task-level performance results. His views on adoption and billing are observations, not a quantified adoption or pricing study, and he explicitly says he does not know the percentage of attorneys using AI. His J-curve explanation invokes economists generally without identifying a study.
For general-purpose competitive pressure, he cites a review by Carolyn Elefant reporting that Claude Cowork can Bates-stamp documents, then draws his own conclusion about erosion of specialist feature advantages. His assessment of content and global deployment draws on Casetext's content limitations and his experience at Thomson Reuters, rather than a comparative content audit.
For reasoning and agentic capabilities, he describes early access to o1, demonstrations, and work with colleagues. The stronger assertion that reasoning would enable anything is a colleague's quoted view, not extracted here as Arredondo's own prediction. He provides no controlled legal-task benchmark for the agentic claims.
For the Massachusetts workflow, he describes the actual task and reports Justice Green's permission to characterize it as successful. He provides no error rate, time saving, sample size, or litigant-outcome measure. Observations about judges' varied adoption and workload arise from his interactions with them.
Separately, Arredondo recounts a University of Chicago study associated with Eric Posner comparing judges and AI on judicial-competence questions, including differently framed presentations of the same facts. He recalls approximately 62% correct for judges and 100% for AI, but explicitly qualifies his recollection and advises reading the study. These are reported study results, not his own measurements or a claim of universal AI superiority over judges.
The proposed BYU collaboration would look for statistical changes in common-law writing; it has not supplied findings in this interview.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Arredondo contrasts early GPT-4 expectations with the situation roughly three years after CoCounsel's launch, while leaving most further developments undated and conditional.
pts.d:
The supplied source is labeled 2026, and the interview looks back approximately three years to CoCounsel's March 2023 launch. Arredondo dates his early GPT-4 access to September 16, 2022. His estimate of dozens of use cases concerns early experimentation, whereas his adoption shortfall concerns progress by the interview date. He stresses both the time required for adoption and continuing model limitations; he does not set a deadline for universal use or changes to legal pricing.
His competitive-threat claim concerns currently emerging general-purpose agents, with future differentiation conditional on specialist vendors adding meaningful value beyond those tools. He advises testing products' functions against general-purpose systems. Content remains important under present conditions, especially where completeness and authoritative treatment matter; he allows that some barriers may erode and that requirements depend on the matter.
His expectation of further agentic advances is prospective but undated, and he withholds details about Thomson Reuters. His assessment of workflow integration acknowledges that unification has begun but remains incomplete.
The Massachusetts project began in the GPT-4 period. Work with other judges on bench memoranda and opinion drafting developed over the preceding year and a half. His willingness to consider opinion drafting is expressly contextual: trial-court overload changed his initial reluctance, while appellate concerns differ. The common-law monitoring project is still being set up, and he does not claim to know the correct overall approach to judicial AI.
On fabricated material, he describes suitable models and human checking as features of responsible attorney use; he does not claim that these eliminate all risk.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are attorneys, legal-tech vendors and content providers, judges and court staff, and people whose disputes are processed through AI-assisted courts.
pts.d:
Attorneys gain access to multiple legal-work functions and potentially more integrated research and document workflows. Arredondo expects increased vendor competition to benefit them but does not quantify savings, productivity, staffing effects, or client-price reductions.
Specialist legal-tech companies, including Harvey and Thomson Reuters/CoCounsel, face competition from foundation-model companies and general-purpose tools. Their challenge is to offer genuinely differentiated legal functionality and content rather than features general-purpose systems already provide. These are software-provider claims, not claims about ALSP market share. Content publishers and aggregators retain relevance because reliable, comprehensive legal materials remain difficult to assemble.
Judges and judicial clerks are both adopters and subjects of concern. The Massachusetts example involves appellate staff handling time-sensitive emergency eviction appeals. Later drafting work concerns other judges, with particularly acute workload pressures described in trial courts. Arredondo distinguishes assistance with summaries, research and drafting from the broader question of how AI may influence the law courts produce; he does not advocate autonomous adjudication.
Litigants in emergency eviction proceedings are indirectly affected by the processing workflow, but the source reports no measured improvement in case outcomes or access to representation. The wider public may be affected by changes to common-law development, which Arredondo wants monitored. The interview does not supply concrete predictions about junior-lawyer displacement, law-firm staffing structures, or the disappearance of hourly billing.
